messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] NA's in x. What to do?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] NA's in x. What to do?
messages.body_plain:
The model you're starting with doesn't actually provide
a model of the predictors in x that are missing.  For any
kind of full Bayesian analysis, that's where you'd need
to start.  So you'd need a full joint model.

https://stat.duke.edu/node/14480

Unfortunately, as Ben pointed out, even if you had a model,
the missingness patterns you have appear to be difficult.

Andrew Gelman and Jennifer Hill have an approach to multiple imputation
which is implemented in the mi system in R:

http://www.stat.ucla.edu/~yajima/Publication/mipaper.rev04.pdf

I believe Ben's taken over the code from Yu-sung Su.

- Bob

On 6/1/13 1:00 AM, Josef Fruehwald wrote:
> Thanks! That did the trick. Frankly, I didn't realize that I could use <lower , upper> restrictions on matrices as well.

We only added this feature fairly recently.  The
syntax is rather clunky, but we wanted to keep
size declarations for arrays, matrices and vectors
to a consistent square brackets notation.

The reason you can remove constant uniform distributions for
parameters is that they have implicit uniform distributions
on their declared support.

- Bob

messages.subject: Speed comparison stan vs MCMCglmm for hierarchical regression
messages.subject_clean: Speed comparison stan vs MCMCglmm for hierarchical regression
messages.body_plain:
I mentioned on Andrew's blog that I had not had good results with stan v1.0 in high dimension, and he suggested I try again and post here.

The setup is a hierarchical regression model with two groups of random effects, one with 100 members and one with 150 members with 900 total individuals. The numbers from from a real dataset that I don't have permission to share, but I simulate data with similar characteristics. I try out both a continuous and binary outcome. I haven't done any real tuning, but have done the obvious things recommended in the manual.  The design matrices are somewhat sparse, and I know that MCMCglmm uses sparse matrix techniques. I didn't see an option for those in stan, or if eigen does so automatically.

The competitor is MCMCglmm, which uses a specialized block-gibbs sampler for regression problems. I dedicate 10% of the iterations to warmup and burnin for each. The results are that (r)stan 1.3 is quite a bit better than I recall from 1.0. The engines are similar on this small test, but I haven't dedicated the CPU time to do numerous replications.

On continuous outcomes (a LMM) MCMCglmm is a bit faster (6.4 effective samples / sec vs 4.1 ES/s), and that the variation of stan is higher (on three trials the minimum ES/s was 1.8; watching the counter go the iteration number has a propensity to go quickly in streaks).

On binary outcomes (a GLMM), stan does better than MCMCglmm with the slice sampling option (2.6 ES/s vs 1.4 ES/s), which is superior to not slice sampling. Again, fairly variable ES/s.

Attached are scripts for both tests and a session info.

Is this a problem likely to benefit from tuning in the warmup or mass matrix options?

Thanks,
Ryan King
University of Chicago Pritzker School of Medicine

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Speed comparison stan vs MCMCglmm for hierarchical regression
messages.body_plain:
Thanks so much for following up.  The main reason for
the speedup from Stan 1.0 to 1.3 is that we've vectorized
the distributions.

Your models look about as efficient as they can
be coded in Stan.  (There is an extra N-vector declaration
in the models for mu, but that shouldn't slow things
down noticeably.)

We've also noticed the high variation among chains for timing.
Part of it is initialization --- we use very diffuse initializations.
You might want to try it with init=0, which centers the initializations.
Even though they're centered to start (on the unconstrained scale),
they'll immediately get a random kick for the initial momentum.

We are working on adaptation with the goal of bringing down
the variation among chain timings.

- Bob

No, thanks for reminding me! I was using stan's n_eff printout and coda:effectiveSize. Using coda:effectiveSize for stan is slightly more generous for the binary outcome (3.1 ES/s).
Oddly enough, it made the continuous outcome look worse (2.7 ES/s). I ran that sampler again to make sure it wasn't a fluke.

It is impressive that stan does about the same on gaussian outcomes and binary ones; binary outcomes are generally a much harder computation problem. Do you think it's a shortcoming of coda:effectiveSize? It's not clear how to access the function rstan is using for n_eff. I also noticed that longer warmup (1000) and run times (10k) tended to produce higher ESS than short ones (500 and 5000).

This is the correct way to access the ESS?
(effectiveSize(fit1@sim$samples[[1]]$effect2sd) +  effectiveSize(fit1@sim$samples[[1]]$effect1sd)) /2

Thanks,
Ryan King

messages.body_plain:
It's easy to use monitor() which is in rstan.  It goes like this:
1.  If the number of iterations per chain is "iter", and the number of chains is "chains", and the number of parameters saved your mcmc output is "d", store the simulations as a 3-way array of dimensions iter, chains, d (in that order).
2.  Suppose those chains have been saved into a 3-way array called sims, and let warmup be the number of warmup iterations.  Then just do monitor (sims, warmup).

It's all obtainable by doing the following in R:
library ("rstan")
help (monitor)

I really really don't want people to be using coda for comparisons!
A

On Monday, June 3, 2013 4:21:54 PM UTC-4, jacktanner wrote:
> I'm creating a large-ish matrix in the transformed data block, and I want to make sure that it is correct. If I use print() statements in the transformed data block, then the large-ish matrix scrolls off the R terminal and is too painful to verify visually. Is there a way to have the print() statements output to a file?

I have a hard time thinking of a case where it would be necessary to do more than verify the first and last rows of the big matrix. And if the matrix has too many columns to easily read, then verifying just the first and last column of the first and last rows ought to be sufficient.

If for some reason that I am currently unable to think of, you really do need to check every single element, I suppose you could create a matrix in the generated quantities block that simply copied the datamatrix. Although then you would have as many "realizations" of the copied matrix as there were post-warmup iterations.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Speed comparison stan vs MCMCglmm for hierarchical regression
messages.body_plain:
On 6/3/13 5:10 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> It's easy to use monitor() which is in rstan.  It goes like this:
> 1.  If the number of iterations per chain is "iter", and the number of chains is "chains", and the number of parameters saved your mcmc output is "d", store the simulations as a 3-way array of dimensions iter, chains, d (in that order).
> 2.  Suppose those chains have been saved into a 3-way array called sims, and let warmup be the number of warmup iterations.  Then just do monitor (sims, warmup).
>
> It's all obtainable by doing the following in R:
> library ("rstan")
> help (monitor)
>
> I really really don't want people to be using coda for comparisons!

I didn't realize that there was a function that could do this
in RStan, but indeed monitor() is just what's needed to compute
summaries of samples and it's very clearly documented.  I just
hadn't seen it.

I don't think there's really a need to do this kind of
thing in command-line Stan.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: debugging transformed data
messages.body_plain:
On 6/3/13 8:26 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Monday, June 3, 2013 4:21:54 PM UTC-4, jacktanner wrote:
>
>     I'm creating a large-ish matrix in the transformed data block, and I want to make sure that it is correct. If I use
>     print() statements in the transformed data block, then the large-ish matrix scrolls off the R terminal and is too
>     painful to verify visually. Is there a way to have the print() statements output to a file?
>
>
> I have a hard time thinking of a case where it would be necessary to do more than verify the first and last rows of the
> big matrix. And if the matrix has too many columns to easily read, then verifying just the first and last column of the
> first and last rows ought to be sufficient.
>
> If for some reason that I am currently unable to think of, you really do need to check every single element, I suppose
> you could create a matrix in the generated quantities block that simply copied the datamatrix. Although then you would
> have as many "realizations" of the copied matrix as there were post-warmup iterations.

No, there's not a way to print to a file, nor do we plan to
add such a method any time soon.

How are you going to verify the transformed data is right if it's
printed to a file?

Can you code the verification up programatically in Stan?  The transformed
data block only gets executed once, so you should feel free to
carry out some heavy computations.   Easy checks would be things
like the matrices being positive or no entries being NaN.  Or even
pairs of rows being orthogonal to within some tolerance.

The data type constraints are automatically checked (for instance,
positive-definiteness for a covariance matrix, or being non-negative
and adding up to 1 for a simplex).

I think it'd be helpful to have something like a way to quit
out of Stan gracefully with an error report.  Like maybe

    exit(...)

with the same arbitrary number of arguments to print as print().

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: column vector
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, June 4, 2013 7:07:52 PM UTC-4, Yilong wrote:
> Hi:
>
> I suppose someone might have asked this question before, however I could not find it in the mailing list. While setting a multivariate normal distribution, I need to declare a vector column from this distribution. Eg.
>
> real tmp[M,N]
>
> tmp[,i] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma)    ( use R's syntax )

If you are doing things like multi_normal(), you don't want to use a plain two-dimensional array (e.g. real tmp[M,N]). Often the fastest is to create a N-array of vectors

vector[M] tmp[N]

in which case you can access the i-th "column" with tmp[i].

The most intuitive (but slightly slower) way to do it from an R perspective is to declare a matrix

matrix[M,N] tmp;

in which case you can access (a copy of) the i-th column with col(tmp, i).

Ben

> vector[M] tmp[N]

If you absolutely don't want to mess with the input format,
you can define this array in the transformed data block.

> The most intuitive (but slightly slower) way to do it from an R perspective is to declare a matrix
>
> |
> matrix[M,N] tmp;
> |
>
> in which case you can access (a copy of) the i-th column with col(tmp, i).

The copy here is just an implementation detail that means it's
a bit slower.  It will behave the same way in a Stan model
as using an array of vectors.

As far as efficiency, given that it's showing up in the context
of a multi-normal, it probably won't be too noticeable.

I like the array of vectors because it seems clearer conceptually
than a matrix, though of course, you can think of a matrix as
an array of vectors.

- Bob

messages.subject: estimating memory requirements
messages.body_plain:
I'm about to run a model on a multi-core Linux box with 16G RAM. I'd
like to run multiple chains in parallel, as in Reference Manual sec 4.2.
But I want to avoid running out of RAM / swapping to disk.

Is it reasonable to estimate the memory requirements for one chain by
running a chain for just some small number of iterations? In other
words, does a Stan model's memory use grow over time, or does it
allocate all the memory it'll need by the end of so-many early
iterations? And if the latter is true, how many iterations do I need for
this estimate?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] estimating memory requirements
messages.body_plain:
Your plan for estimating memory usage should work just fine for Stan.  The amount of memory used shouldn't grow over iterations, although it's a good idea to let it run for a few iterations before checking memory usage to ensure that the full NUTS tree depth has been hit.  That said, for most complex models the amount of memory used by the sampler is dwarfed by the amount used by the autodiff so even one iteration should get you pretty close.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] os x rstan compilation failure
messages.body_plain:
Your .Rprofile outputs a lot of stuff, which becomes part of the makefile for installing RStan as it uses Rscript to find some files in Rcpp.  Currently the easy solution for you is to let R not use this .Rprofile (for example, renaming it temporarily).

messages.subject: writing intermediate variables declared in the model block?
messages.subject_clean: writing intermediate variables declared in the model block?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan team,

Thanks for all your hard work - Stan is a great tool!

My question is about writing (ie. saving) an intermediate variable declared in the model block. This variable is a function of other variables defined in the model block as well as parameters. I don't seem to be able to declare it in earlier blocks (but perhaps I am missing something and can in fact do this). From what I understand, I can write it in generated quantities, but this requires redefining most of my local model variables (that I don't want written) and copying a large portion of the model block in order to build up to this variable from the sampled parameters. I assume if I did all this it would slow my program down considerably...

Is there any way write an intermediate variable like this? The variable I want to write is shown below as g. It depend on the parameter alpha, but it also depends on H[k] which is in turn a functions of some covariance matrices that depend on parameters (negative exponential covariance function).

####
  for (k in 1:W) {
    alpha[k] ~ multi_normal(zeros, C_star[k]);
    g[k] <- mu[k]*ones + H[k]*alpha[k];
  }
####

In case it helps to understand my question, my model is attached. I'm modelling counts of tree species across space using predictive process model. Counts are multinomial, and the proportions are obtained by transforming the latent gaussian process values. I would like to write my process values (g in my code) or proportions (r in my code), and perhaps there is an easy way to do this that you can direct me to. Simulated data is attached as well.

(I am aware that I could instead be sampling g instead of sampling alpha earlier on, in which case I could easily write g, but was having trouble with positive definiteness so opted to sample after the fewest number of matrix operations to avoid numerical errors.)

Thanks so much!

Andria

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] writing intermediate variables declared in the model block?
messages.body_plain:
On 6/7/13 12:49 AM, Andria Dawson wrote:
> Hi Stan team,
>
> Thanks for all your hard work - Stan is a great tool!
>
> My question is about writing (ie. saving) an intermediate variable declared in the model block. This variable is a
> function of other variables defined in the model block as well as parameters. I don't seem to be able to declare it in
> earlier blocks (but perhaps I am missing something and can in fact do this).

Any variable defined in the model block can be defined in the
transformed parameters block.  The key requirement is that all
of the variables on which it depends must also be defined in
the transformed parameters block.

Any variables that you don't need in the model block can be
declared as local in the transformed parameters block by putting
them at the beginning of a statement block, like this:

transformed parameters {
    real z;    // visible to model, printed
    {
       real y; // local, invisible to model, not printed
       y <- ... some calculation involving  data and parameters ...;
       z <- ... some calculation involving y ...;
    }
}

I'm attaching a version of your model that manages to not
do anything redundantly, but it's also going to print
C_star, which can be a dealbreaker as it looks larger than anything
else being printed.

(I also took the liberty of vectorizing and reformatting a bit.)

We really need to work on marking transformed parameters as
optional for printing, which is the right way to solve this problem.

> From what I understand, I can write it in
> generated quantities, but this requires redefining most of my local model variables (that I don't want written) and
> copying a large portion of the model block in order to build up to this variable from the sampled parameters. I assume
> if I did all this it would slow my program down considerably...

Probably not.  The sampling is much slower than the
intermediate calculations, so you might not even notice
the recalculation time.

But the redefinition is a deal breaker.  Repeating code
is a bad idea because it can get out of synch and even
if it doesn't, it makes the program harder to read.

> Is there any way write an intermediate variable like this? The variable I want to write is shown below as g. It depend
> on the parameter alpha, but it also depends on H[k] which is in turn a functions of some covariance matrices that depend
> on parameters (negative exponential covariance function).
>
> ####
>    for (k in 1:W) {
>      alpha[k] ~ multi_normal(zeros, C_star[k]);
>      g[k] <- mu[k]*ones + H[k]*alpha[k];
>    }
> ####
>
> In case it helps to understand my question, my model is attached. I'm modelling counts of tree species across space
> using predictive process model. Counts are multinomial, and the proportions are obtained by transforming the latent
> gaussian process values. I would like to write my process values (g in my code) or proportions (r in my code), and
> perhaps there is an easy way to do this that you can direct me to. Simulated data is attached as well.
>
> (I am aware that I could instead be sampling g instead of sampling alpha earlier on, in which case I could easily write
> g, but was having trouble with positive definiteness so opted to sample after the fewest number of matrix operations to
> avoid numerical errors.)

Ben or Marcus may be able to help with matrix stability issues.

Marcus has some speedups for Gaussian processes that are going
into our next release.

You should check my work here, but I think you can also replace
this:

     // construct H

     for (k in 1:W) {

       L[k] <- cholesky_decompose(C_star[k]);
       L_inv[k] <- inverse(L[k]);
       C_star_inv[k] <- crossprod(L_inv[k]);
       H[k] <- c[k] * C_star_inv[k];
     }

with:

   for (k in 1:W)

     H[k] <- c[k] / C_star[k];

What I'm not sure about is whether this is a better form for
the algebra given that we know C_star is positive definite.

> Thanks so much!

You're welcome.

- Bob

Ideally we could add a type modifier like:

Andria, definitely post if you're seeing numerical stability issues.  Some of them we know about but many of them we don't.  Plus, seeing users run into them can be motivating to getting things fixed :)

>

> into our next release.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] 'Matt trick' for logistic-binomial model
messages.body_plain:
A serious problem with your model is that you declare
sigma2 as having support (0,infinity)

   real<lower=0> sigma2;

and then you use it with bounded support:

   sigma2 ~ uniform(0,100);

What you need to do is declare sigma2 with support
that matches the model.

   real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma2;

The re-encoding in model2 forgot the additive term for
the mean.  Instead of

transformed parameters {
   real u[G];
   for (g in 1:G)
     u[g] <- e_u[g] * sqrt(sigma2);
}

you need the assignment to include the mean u0:

   for (g in 1:G)
     u[g] <- u0 + e_u[g] * sqrt(sigma2);

but you really want to declare e_u as a vector:

    vector[G] e_u;

and then vectorize the assignment:

    u <- u0 + e_u * sqrt(sigma2);

In fact, for both speed and simplicity, I'd replace
prior for variance

   sigma2 ~ uniform(0,100);

with a uniform prior on standard deviation (changing the
constraint on its support to upper=10, of course!):

   sigma ~ uniform(0,10);

and then replace the vectorized assignment with

   u <- u0 + e_u * sigma;

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bob and Andrew,

Thanks for the helpful suggestions.  Right after I posted I realized that I had forgotten to incude the u0 term in the transformed parameters block.  I tried to pull the post once I realized my mistake.  After I put the mean term back in, things worked more or less as expected in terms of the estimates from the posterior.

If you don't mind, I have a couple of follow up questions...

1.  Andrew, is Bob's suggestion of using uniform(0,10) for sigma more in line with what you had in mind or were you thinking of something else?

2.  The effective sample size on all of the terms involved with transformed parameter block are surprisingly low.  I've attached the code (updated based on your suggestions) and results from a run using 4 chains with 10K iterations apiece.  Any thoughts on what is going on here?  While I'm definitely concerned about the effective sample size associated with sigma and u0, is there any need to worry about the e_u terms, or can we safely set these aside as a byproduct of the Matt trick. In short, do we expect viable sample sizes for things like the e_u terms?

3.  I ran into the Matt trick while looking into ways of speeding up the model.  One possibility is to run this in JAGS which has a dedicated glm module.  In discussing this point in another thread <https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!topic/stan-users/QDumPPbRa4Q>, Matt Hoffman alluded to the possibility of using the Matt trick in JAGS.  I decided to check this out, but started getting totally off-the-wall estimates for sigma.  As suggested by my original post, it is totally possible that I just goofed up the code (see attached).  If you have any thoughts, I'd love to hear them, though you should feel free to tell me to take a hike given that this is a Stan list and I can understand that you might not want to accidentally encourage possible defection, even if only in the very short term.  Even if you don't feel comfortable commenting on the JAGS code, is there any reason to believe that the Matt trick would be viable in one program but another?  I could imagine situations in which it didn't do much with respect to speed, but I have a tougher time seeing how it could actually produce nonsensical results.

Thanks again for all of your help.  All of these questions aside, Stan is a fine piece of software and I look forward to seeing where it goes.

Adam

If you think this is a serious problem for the purposes of this discussion, I'm happy to go back and recalculate things.  Looking at these rough estimates, however, not only does JAGS seem to outpace Stan, but Stan without the Matt trick seems to better than Stan with the Matt trick.

Just to be clear about a couple of things...

1.  Times for Stan do not include the time taken to compile the models.
2.  I made sure to use set_cppo("fast"), though this type of thing wouldn't explain the divergence between alternative parameterizations in Stan.

What else could I be missing here?

Adam

On 6/7/13 6:35 PM, Adam Slez wrote:
...

> 2.  The effective sample size on all of the terms involved with transformed parameter block are surprisingly low.  I've
> attached the code (updated based on your suggestions) and results from a run using 4 chains with 10K iterations apiece.

>   Any thoughts on what is going on here?  While I'm definitely concerned about the effective sample size associated with
> sigma and u0, is there any need to worry about the e_u terms, or can we safely set these aside as a byproduct of the
> Matt trick. In short, do we expect viable sample sizes for things like the e_u terms?

Are you doing this through bin/print or using RStan?

I'm curious about what's going on here conceptually.

With the Matt trick, you sample

   e_u ~ normal(0,1)

and then set:

   u <- u0 + sigma * e_u

u0, sigma, and e_u all have low n_eff (< 70)
whereas u has a high n_eff (2,000).

Is it the extra variability of the three variables combined
that gives u relatively low autocorrelation?

It also looks like some of the u0 have too high R-hat (1.16),
which I wouldn't expect after so many iterations.
So it's possible one of the chains just got stuck with your
initialization.  You can try init=0, which is more like what
you get with JAGS if you don't initialize yourself.  Could
you also send the traceplot for u0, bx, and sigma?

Do the traceplots show high correlation of the u0, sigma,
and e_u variables?  Are the posterior variances the same
in Stan and JAGS?

Andrew?

> 3.  I ran into the Matt trick while looking into ways of speeding up the model.  One possibility is to run this in JAGS
> which has a dedicated glm module.  In discussing this point in another thread

> <https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups#!topic/stan-users/QDumPPbRa4Q>, Matt Hoffman alluded to the possibility of

> using the Matt trick in JAGS.  I decided to check this out, but started getting totally off-the-wall estimates for
> sigma.

I'd check in with Martyn Plummer on the JAGS list to see
if JAGS will sample properly through the assignments.
I don't see why not, but I don't know for sure it can
calculate the right Markov blanket.

I'd also check if the Matt trick will interfere with the GLM.

For Stan, there's nothing special done for GLMs and the Matt
trick works because of the way Stan works by just defining
the log probability function.

> As suggested by my original post, it is totally possible that I just goofed up the code (see attached).

It looks OK to me.  And I don't see an obvious way to
make it more efficient.

None of the scales look that crazy, so I'm also wondering if
many of the predictors are correlated.

> I could imagine situations in which it [the Matt trick] didn't do much with

> respect to speed, but I have a tougher time seeing how it could actually produce nonsensical results.

There are so many ways things can go wrong and produce
nonsensical results.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bob, Ben, and Andrew,

I redid the analysis used to produce the previous speed tests which, I forgot to mention, were only based on 2K iterations (hence why some of the R-hats were so high).  Here's what is going on in the setup of the new tests:

1.  I used 4 chains with 10K iterations.

2.  I estimated three additional models.  As per Bob's suggestion, the first uses the Matt trick as before, but initial values are set to zero.  The second uses the Matt trick, but the x variable has been mean centered via the use of a transformed data block.  The third model also uses a mean-centered x, but does not use the Matt trick.

3.  Output was produced using the monitor command so as to ensure comparability between Stan and JAGS, as per the discussion here.  This speaks to Bob's question regarding the calculation of effective sample size.  One thing I noticed is that the monitor results did not match the print results.  I might expect this when looking at the JAGS output, but this also happened in Stan as well.  My understanding is that the print output in Stan is based on the summary function.  How do the summary calculations differ from the monitor calculations?

Here's my reading of the findings:

1.  JAGS outpaces Stan by quite a bit, regardless of how the model is specified in Stan.

2.  Stan models which use the Matt trick seem to do worse than Stan models without the Matt trick.

3.  Models with and without the Matt trick differ in terms of which parameters they are able to efficiently estimate.  Models with the Matt trick do better with respect to bx as compared to u0 or sigma.  The opposite holds for models without the Matt trick.

4.  Mean centering doesn't seem to help much.

5.  To speak to Bob's earlier question, in terms of posterior variance Stan actually seems to be doing slightly better when we look at the standard deviation.  Things are obviously a bit different when we look at, say, the standard error of the mean which corrects for effective sample size. Overall, JAGS seems to be doing better here, in large part because of the fact that Stan does well with either u0 and sigma or bx, but not both.  More specifically, we see Stan without the Matt trick doing better than JAGS with to the standard error of the mean for u0 and sigma.  In contrast, if we either center x or set initial values to 0, we see Stan with the Matt trick doing better than JAGS with respect to the standard error of the mean for bx.

I have also attached the diagnostics requested by Bob and Ben.  These include both a traceplot for u0, sigma, and bx, as well as the pairs graph depicting chain-specific results (chains 1 and 2 are on the first page, while chains 3 and 4 are on the second).  To show the correlation between parameter estimates, I have also included a scatterplot matrix depicting draws for u0, sigma, bx, and five randomly chosen group effects (both transformed and untransformed). I'm not sure whether this is the best approach for answering Bob's question as to whether the traceplots show high correlation of the u0, sigma, and e_u variables.  In the first place, I'm not sure that what I did even counts as a traceplot in the usual sense. It would also be preferable to look at all of the u and e_u terms, but I couldn't think of a good way to do this given that I have 144 groups and, hence, 288 + 3 = 291 parameters to graph.  All graphs correspond to the row in the table labeled "Stan w/Matt" (i.e. I used the Matt trick but did not center x or force initial values to 0).

My read is that the chains for u0 and sigma aren't mixing especially well (at least not compared to bx) and that there is some correlation between sigma, u, and e_u, though maybe not a crazy amount.  The u terms seem okay, there is some evidence of correlation between sigma and the e_u terms, and there is definitely correlation among the e_u terms themselves.  Again, this approach is less than perfect because I'm only looking at a handful of u/e_u terms.  Things could be worse elsewhere in the model.

Adam

messages.subject: Cauchy vs. uniform priors for scales
messages.subject_clean: Cauchy vs. uniform priors for scales
messages.body_plain:
Cauchy's just like any other prior.  It's in the manual
section on regression and also documented in the distributions.
In Stan:

   parameters {
     real<lower=0> sigma;
   ...
   model {
     sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
   ...

In JAGS, you just need to truncate, so it'd be this
if they have the cauchy

    sigma ~ dcauchy(0,5) T[0,];

and otherwise you'll need to replace dcauchy with the
T distribution with 1 degree of freedom.

You need to truncate for the uniform in JAGS, too.

- Bob

Very good question.  Jiqiang and Daniel should know.

One issue is going to be whether the warmup iterations get included.
They should NOT be included in estimating means and variances and
MCMC error.

> Here's my reading of the findings:
>
> 1.  JAGS outpaces Stan by quite a bit, regardless of how the model is specified in Stan.

Can you quantify "quite a bit"?

And you're sure that Stan itself was compiled using -O3?  It
should be automatic if you're using the command-line version
and just call "make".  RStan's a bit more probelmatic because your
current R config determines how binary packages get compiled.
We're trying to make this more transparent for the next release.

> 2.  Stan models which use the Matt trick seem to do worse than Stan models without the Matt trick.

It shouldn't really help much at all given the refactorization.

> 5.  To speak to Bob's earlier question, in terms of posterior variance Stan actually seems to be doing slightly better
> when we look at the standard deviation.

Better in that it's estimate is closer to the true values?

Was this simulated data you used or real data?

> Things are obviously a bit different when we look at, say, the standard error
> of the mean which corrects for effective sample size.

I'm not sure what you mean here.  I was talking about estimating the variance,
so it'd be the standard error of the variance estimate we'd care about.

If the variance itself is overestimated or underestimated, it'll throw
off MCMC error by the same amount, of course.

The problem that can show up with either Gibbs or HMC is that the
sampler won't sample into the tails of the posterior, so variance
gets underestimated.

> Overall, JAGS seems to be doing better here, in large part because
> of the fact that Stan does well with either u0 and sigma or bx, but not both.  More specifically, we see Stan without

correlation among u0, sigma, and bx.

fully covered the posterior density properly after 10K samples,

the u0 x sigma scatterplot doesn't look like the transpose of the
sigma x u0 scatterplot.

On the other hand, the coefficients themselves are highly correlated not
only with u0, but with each other.

This problem's small enough that you could deal with this kind of systematic
correlation using a full mass matrix.  (It runs slower per iteration typically,
but can mix better.)

> sure whether this is the best approach for answering Bob's question as to whether the traceplots show high correlation

On Monday, June 10, 2013 10:44:31 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The blown up pairs.pdf indicates that we perhaps haven't even
> fully covered the posterior density properly after 10K samples,
> especially looking at u0 vs. bx.   But I'm confused as to why
> the u0 x sigma scatterplot doesn't look like the transpose of the
> sigma x u0 scatterplot.

TFM says for the chain_id argument to pairs():

> By default, NULL, which will plot roughly half of the chains in the lower panel and the rest in the upper panel. Otherwise, an integer vector can be passed to select some subset of the chains, of which roughly half will be plotted in the lower panel and the rest in the upper panel. Or a list of two integer vectors, each specifying a subset of the chains to be plotted in the lower and upper panels respectively. The latter option can be useful if you suspect that one chain has failed to converge.

So, the i-j plot will never be identical to the j-i plot, unless you do something wasteful like chain_id = c(1,1). I'm not sure exactly what was passed for this plot, but if the i-j plot looks substantially different than the j-i plot, then it didn't converge.

Ben

In terms of u0 and sigma, JAGS appears to be producing at least twice as many effective samples per second.  In terms of bx, JAGS appears to be doing at least seven times as many effective samples per second.  This doesn't account for the monitor issue. > And you're sure that Stan itself was compiled using -O3?  It

> and just call "make".  RStan's a bit more probelmatic because your
> current R config determines how binary packages get compiled.

>

I'll be honest and say I'm not sure.  I've been running everything using RStan which I installed using the steps shown on the Getting Started page.  For the most part I've been using 64-bit Rstan on a MacBook Pro with set_cppo(mode = "fast").  I've also tried running things on a 32-bit Windows machine, though that seemed to do worse, not to mention the fact that I get crazy long warnings starting with MSDOS paths being detected and ending with 'void stan::agrad::free_memory()' defined but not used.  Though everything runs exactly the same despite these warnings, I've mostly stuck to running things on the Mac as a result.

> > when we look at the standard deviation.
>

>

No.  I just meant that the estimated standard deviation of the posterior (as reported via monitor) was smaller in the Stan output than in the JAGS output.  I wasn't sure what you are asking for and this was my best guess.  Based on your original email and your response above, I see that you were looking for variance as opposed to the standard deviation.  I was being a bit lazy and working with the default output.  It wouldn't be too hard to go back and calculate the variance instead, assuming that I correctly understand what you are asking for.

> Was this simulated data you used or real data?
>

This is real data.

>
> > Things are obviously a bit different when we look at, say, the standard error
> > of the mean which corrects for effective sample size.
>
> I'm not sure what you mean here.  I was talking about estimating the variance,
> so it'd be the standard error of the variance estimate we'd care about.
>

Again, I wasn't totally sure what you were looking for and this was a bad, nonsensical guess on my part. My thought was basically that the standard of the mean is going to be a function of the standard deviation of the posterior and, hence, might tell us about how spread out things are (assuming that a high standard deviation might indicate that a chain has run off in the opposite direction), though I suspect that this is not the right way to think about the problem given that similarities and differences in the standard error of the mean could be driven the effective sample size as opposed to the standard deviation.

> To recreate this error, run the stan file "pls_posdef_error.stan" with the data "fit_data.dump" containing the list called fit_data

Stan requires a strictly positive definite covariance matrix.

For Gaussian processes with non-full-rank covariance due to
equal inputs, you need to add noise (what Radford Neal called
jitter).  There's a discussion in the manual.

Also, can set_cppo("debug") mess up other binary installs for user's
R packages?

Sorry to keep harping on this point, but my experience is that if there's
a way for a user to mess something up that doesn't flash warnings in
large red lights, then it's going to get messed up by at least a fraction
of the users.

Also, I have some idea how clunky the R build process is for packages.
I wish they didn't have global overrides, but I suppose that's the way R
sets most things up.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: BUGS Example Vol 2 Stagnant Problem
messages.body_plain:
The real issue is that Stan doesn't support integer parameters.
One approach is to take the poor parameterization of BUGS and
marginalize out the integer parameter k.  Because k is a top
level parameter, this requires summing out at the very top level
of the model.  The manual has more info on how to do this in the
mixture model chapter -- you need to use log_sum_exp.

They also have a continuous version of the model:

  http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/winbugs/Vol2.pdf

I'll try both versions and report back.  It'd be nice
to complete our collection of BUGS models :-)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: BUGS Example Vol 2 Stagnant Problem
messages.body_plain:
Here's a model that marginalizes out the discrete mixture-component identifier
of the BUGS "stagnant" model.

First, the BUGS model for comparison, which I took along with their output
from:

http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/winbugs/Vol2.pdf

model {

  for (i in 1:N) {

    Y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i],tau)
    mu[i] <- alpha + beta[J[i]] * (x[i] - x[k])
    J[i] <- 1 + step(i - k - 0.5)
    punif[i] <- 1/N
  }
  tau ~ dgamma(0.001,0.001)
  alpha ~ dnorm(0.0,1.0E-6)
  for (j in 1:2)
    beta[j] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.0E-6)
  k ~ dcat(punif[])

  sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau)
}

And here's the Stan version that marginalizes out k with a mixture
parameter theta:

// Bradley P. Carlin; Alan E. Gelfand; Adrian F. M. Smith.
// Hierarchical Bayesian Analysis of Changepoint Problems
// Applied Statistics, Vol. 41, No. 2. (1992), pp. 389-405.
//
// In these data, X represents the logarithm of the flow rate of
// water down an inclined channel (grams per centimetre per second)
// and Y represents the logarithm of the height of the stagnant
// surface layer (centimetres) for different surfactants.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real x[N];
  real Y[N];
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  real<lower=0> alpha;
  real beta[2];
  simplex[N] theta;
}
model {
  // local variables
  real log_probs[N];
  real mu[N];

  // priors
  theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(0.01,N));
  alpha  ~ normal(0,5);
  beta ~ normal(0,5);

  // mixture likelihood
  for (k in 1:N) {

    for (n in 1:N)

      mu[n] <- alpha + if_else(n <= k, beta[1], beta[2]) * (x[n] - x[k]);
    log_probs[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(Y, mu, sigma);
  }
  lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log_probs);
}

Things to note:

1.  I reparameterized from precision to std deviation.

2.  I tightened the priors on the coefficients from sd=1000 to sd=5.

3.  I marginalized out the mixture component indicator k from the original
model and gave it a Dirichlet distribution.  The model is actually very
sensitive to the Dirichlet(gamma) prior.

4.  The posterior is very sensitive to the Dirichlet prior on the mixture.
With the Dirichlet prior set to a symmetric 0.01 prior count, the answers
are roughly the same as BUGS (including similar modes at alpha=0.5 and change
point k=15 or and alpha=1 and changepoint k = 8.  Values for the other parameters
are similar to what was reported in the BUGS volume 2 description.

Here's the print from RStan for a single chain with prior = 0.01 as in the
model above, where you can see the sampling's
still not great.  Convergence is very fast (20 or 30 iterations), but mixing remains
slow after convergence.  You can see the change point estimated to be in the 14-16
range with 75% posterior probability, which matches the traceplot in BUGS in the
mode of alpha = 0.5.

On Jun 11, 2013, at 4:28 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> Here's a model that marginalizes out the discrete mixture-component identifier
> of the BUGS "stagnant" model.
>
> First, the BUGS model for comparison, which I took along with their output
> from:
>
> http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/bugs/winbugs/Vol2.pdf
>
> model {
>   for (i in 1:N) {
>     Y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i],tau)
>     mu[i] <- alpha + beta[J[i]] * (x[i] - x[k])
>     J[i] <- 1 + step(i - k - 0.5)
>     punif[i] <- 1/N
>   }
>   tau ~ dgamma(0.001,0.001)
>   alpha ~ dnorm(0.0,1.0E-6)
>   for (j in 1:2)
>     beta[j] ~ dnorm(0.0,1.0E-6)
>   k ~ dcat(punif[])
>   sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau)
> }
>
> And here's the Stan version that marginalizes out k with a mixture
> parameter theta:
>
> // Bradley P. Carlin; Alan E. Gelfand; Adrian F. M. Smith.
> // Hierarchical Bayesian Analysis of Changepoint Problems
> // Applied Statistics, Vol. 41, No. 2. (1992), pp. 389-405.
> //
> // In these data, X represents the logarithm of the flow rate of
> // water down an inclined channel (grams per centimetre per second)
> // and Y represents the logarithm of the height of the stagnant
> // surface layer (centimetres) for different surfactants.
>
> data {
>   int<lower=0> N;
>   real x[N];
>   real Y[N];
> }
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0> sigma;
>   real<lower=0> alpha;
>   real beta[2];
>   simplex[N] theta;
> }
> model {
>   // local variables
>   real log_probs[N];
>   real mu[N];
>
>   // priors
>   theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(0.01,N));
>   alpha  ~ normal(0,5);
>   beta ~ normal(0,5);
>
>   // mixture likelihood
>   for (k in 1:N) {
>     for (n in 1:N)
>       mu[n] <- alpha + if_else(n <= k, beta[1], beta[2]) * (x[n] - x[k]);
>     log_probs[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(Y, mu, sigma);
>   }
>   lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log_probs);
> }
>
> Things to note:
>
> 1.  I reparameterized from precision to std deviation.
>
> 2.  I tightened the priors on the coefficients from sd=1000 to sd=5.
>
> 3.  I marginalized out the mixture component indicator k from the original
> model and gave it a Dirichlet distribution.  The model is actually very
> sensitive to the Dirichlet(gamma) prior.
>
> 4.  The posterior is very sensitive to the Dirichlet prior on the mixture.
> With the Dirichlet prior set to a symmetric 0.01 prior count, the answers
> are roughly the same as BUGS (including similar modes at alpha=0.5 and change
> point k=15 or and alpha=1 and changepoint k = 8.  Values for the other parameters
> are similar to what was reported in the BUGS volume 2 description.
>
> Here's the print from RStan for a single chain with prior = 0.01 as in the
> model above, where you can see the sampling's
> still not great.  Convergence is very fast (20 or 30 iterations), but mixing remains
> slow after convergence.  You can see the change point estimated to be in the 14-16
> range with 75% posterior probability, which matches the traceplot in BUGS in the
> mode of alpha = 0.5.

Here's the continuous version, which fits exactly the same
values to 2 decimal places as BUGS for posterior mean
and deviation, and converges with 4 chains.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real x[N];
  real Y[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
  real<lower=0> alpha;
  real beta[2];

  real<lower=min(x),upper=max(x)> x_change;
}
model {
  real mu[N];

  alpha  ~ normal(0,5);
  beta ~ normal(0,5);

  sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);

  for (n in 1:N)
    mu[n] <- alpha

      + if_else(x[n] < x_change, beta[1], beta[2]) * (x[n] - x_change);
  Y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
}

post-warmup draws per chain=1000, total post-warmup draws=4000.

> //
> // In these data, X represents the logarithm of the flow rate of
> // water down an inclined channel (grams per centimetre per second)
> // and Y represents the logarithm of the height of the stagnant
> // surface layer (centimetres) for different surfactants.
>
> data {
>   int<lower=0> N;
>   real x[N];
>   real Y[N];
> }
> parameters {
>   real<lower=0> sigma;
>   real<lower=0> alpha;
>   real beta[2];
>   simplex[N] theta;
> }
> model {
>   // local variables
>   real log_probs[N];
>   real mu[N];
>
>   // priors
>   theta ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(0.01,N));
>   alpha  ~ normal(0,5);
>   beta ~ normal(0,5);
>
>   // mixture likelihood
>   for (k in 1:N) {
>     for (n in 1:N)
>       mu[n] <- alpha + if_else(n <= k, beta[1], beta[2]) * (x[n] - x[k]);
>     log_probs[k] <- log(theta[k]) + normal_log(Y, mu, sigma);
>   }
>   lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log_probs);
> }
>
> Things to note:
>
> 1.  I reparameterized from precision to std deviation.
>
> 2.  I tightened the priors on the coefficients from sd=1000 to sd=5.
>
> 3.  I marginalized out the mixture component indicator k from the original
> model and gave it a Dirichlet distribution.  The model is actually very
> sensitive to the Dirichlet(gamma) prior.
>
> 4.  The posterior is very sensitive to the Dirichlet prior on the mixture.
> With the Dirichlet prior set to a symmetric 0.01 prior count, the answers
> are roughly the same as BUGS (including similar modes at alpha=0.5 and
> change
> point k=15 or and alpha=1 and changepoint k = 8.  Values for the other
> parameters
> are similar to what was reported in the BUGS volume 2 description.
>
> Here's the print from RStan for a single chain with prior = 0.01 as in the
> model above, where you can see the sampling's
> still not great.  Convergence is very fast (20 or 30 iterations), but
> mixing remains
> slow after convergence.  You can see the change point estimated to be in
> the 14-16
> range with 75% posterior probability, which matches the traceplot in BUGS
> in the
> mode of alpha = 0.5.

messages.subject: Vector vs. Array
Re: Vector vs. Array
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, June 11, 2013 10:50:16 PM UTC-4, Luca Billi wrote:
> However, the example seems to work if the declaration "real x[N]" is replaced by "vector[N] x".
>
> So, I'm wondering whether I'm missing something or the Manual needs to be updated.

The manual is wrong and replacing the array with a vector is reasonable. For the most part, a vector is preferable to a one-dimensional array of reals in the sense that operations like beta * x are defined. However, I think there are some operations that work elementwise on an array but don't work for a vector. The array is necessary for integer data and sometimes a multidimensional array is useful.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

Thoroughly enjoying learning to use STAN.  Thanks so much for all of your efforts.

Not a question from me, but noting down a learning experience in the hopes that it might save someone else some time.

I needed to do some data manipulation in the transformed parameters block of my STAN code but couldn't figure out how to do it without delcaring an integer to use for controlling loops and array alocation.

The solution is that integers can be declared locally in the transformed parameters block. Variables are locally declared by inserting an opening curly brace before declaration and a closing curly brace at the end of the program block.

Thanks again,

Jon.

messages.body_plain:
Please take this with a grain of salt, because I'm not
that familiar with Kalman filters.  There are some
general issues with the model, though.

1.  You have improper uniform priors on all of the regression
coefficients and noise terms.  And on x[1].  Putting priors
on these helps dampen the huge amount of posterior certainty
in this model.

2.  The model does not seem to be identifiable as specified.  Changing
the sign of both x and h_trans leads to the same results.  Constraining
h_trans to be positive seems to help.  But there still seems to be a huge
amount of posterior uncertainty.

3.  Is it OK to have a ftrans = -1.01?  It implies an
oscillation around f_off in the x[n] because

    x[n] ~ normal(f_off + f_trans * x[n-1], f_noise);

I've attached a simulator in R, as well as a revised model

with much stronger priors and a positivity constraint on h_trans.

4.  Even if I constrain f_trans and h_trans to be between 0 and 1
and remove h_off and f_off from the model, there's still a huge
degree of posterior uncerainty.

Part of the problem may be that 100 data points isn't enough
to estimate this model well because of the degrees of freedom.

I used a non-diagonal mass matrix, but that doesn't seem
to make much of a difference.

The model could also be vectorized for speed.

- Bob

Here is a description of my example.  I am fitting my models on simulated data at this stage.  Once i get a model that is working well enough I will make the attempt to apply it to real data.  The model I am sharing here does not converge (I think too much latency, not enough data) so I have more work ahead of me.  What I have loved about STAN so far is that it has enabled me to fail (so far) so quickly.  Someone else tried a similar model using the EM algorithm and there was weeks of development time and several overnight runs to find out it didn't converge.

 I want to predict the probability of a behaviour (e) displayed by entities.  These entities are controlled by one or more directors.  Each director has some level of desire (d) and opportunity (o) for the entity to carry out the behaviour.  The e, d and o all emit some data x_e, x_d and x_o which I have set up as a regression relationship.  Opportunity for a director (o) depends on desire of that director (d) and the behaviour (e) depends on the opportunity and desire of all directors.  The behaviour (e) is observed as a binary variable (e-hat)  I have attached a word document containing a DAG for this model.

My model assumes vague priors for all of the regression parameters.  I assume a beta(1,1) for d.  I use a beta prior for o where the parameters depend on d.  I use a beta prior for e where the parameters depend on d and o.

I use rstan to fit this model.  My session info is pasted in at the end of this post.

I attach an R-script that generates my data, defines my STAN code and runs the model.

Thanks for your interest.

Jon.

Bob,

Thanks.

2013/6/13 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:

> Please take this with a grain of salt, because I'm not
> that familiar with Kalman filters.

Actually in this context it's just a shorthand for a time-series model
with Gaussian updates and Gaussian observations - not much extra to be
familiar with. Also, in the typical Kalman filter, the
update/observation parameters are hard-coded, whereas here I was
hoping to infer them - too optimistic.

> There are some
> general issues with the model, though.
>
> 1.  You have improper uniform priors on all of the regression
> coefficients and noise terms.  And on x[1].  Putting priors
> on these helps dampen the huge amount of posterior certainty
> in this model.

Thanks. Wanted to leave priors on the coefficients improper (to see if
it would work anyway), but that's nonsense for the noise terms in
particular since the hidden time series needs _some_ kind of anchoring
to the observations.

> 2.  The model does not seem to be identifiable as specified.  Changing
> the sign of both x and h_trans leads to the same results.  Constraining
> h_trans to be positive seems to help.  But there still seems to be a huge
> amount of posterior uncertainty.

That positivity constraint is undesirable in general, but yes I do
need to break the symmetry somewhere. I can do this by having an
off-centre prior on h_trans.

> 3.  Is it OK to have a ftrans = -1.01?  It implies an
> oscillation around f_off in the x[n] because
>
>     x[n] ~ normal(f_off + f_trans * x[n-1], f_noise);

Yes, oscillation is fine, and deliberate.

> I've attached a simulator in R, as well as a revised model
> with much stronger priors and a positivity constraint on h_trans.
>
> 4.  Even if I constrain f_trans and h_trans to be between 0 and 1
> and remove h_off and f_off from the model, there's still a huge
> degree of posterior uncerainty.
>
> Part of the problem may be that 100 data points isn't enough
> to estimate this model well because of the degrees of freedom.
>
> I used a non-diagonal mass matrix, but that doesn't seem
> to make much of a difference.
>
> The model could also be vectorized for speed.

I don't want it to run fast though. Gives me a chance to catch up ;)

Thanks
Dan

On Friday, June 14, 2013 2:21:01 AM UTC-4, Dieter Menne wrote:
> In case the manual should be edited:

It should be.

> It would be nice to have some comments on "When to use real[] and when to use a vector" in the manual. For me it was unexpected that setting priors on real[] was possible without a loop, so this is vector-like behavior. And why are (all? sorry, if I should have missed it) parameters to/from R are passed as real/int[], and not as vectors.

I would say: Use a vector unless you have to use an array. The cases where you have to use an array are when the data are integer valued and when you want to use a 3+ dimensional structure.  For two dimensional, you can use a matrix (of reals only).

It is sometimes useful to utilize an array that contains something other than a real, i.e. you can have an array of vectors (which is somewhat like a matrix but without many matrix algebra capabilities) an array of matrices, etc. But a one dimensional array of reals is not that useful. Sometimes you will run into a function that operates elementwise over the whole array of reals while that function does not operate elementwise over a vector, matrix, etc. In that case, you have to write the loop explicitly in your .stan file, but that doesn't really waste any time.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Kalman filter in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Roweis and Gharamani (1999) explain these models
and what's needed to identify them:

  http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~liam/teaching/neurostat-spr12/papers/hmm/roweis-ghahramani-lds.pdf

The observation noise needs to be set to 1.0 because otherwise
the scale of the coefficient on the observation isn't identified.

So here's a model that works (also attached):

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector[N] y;
}
parameters {
  vector[N] x;
  real f_off;
  real f_trans;
  real h_off;
  real h_trans;
  real<lower=0> h_noise;
}
model {
  f_off ~ normal(0,1);
  f_trans ~ normal(0,1);
  h_off ~ normal(0,1);
  h_trans ~ normal(0,1);
  h_noise ~ normal(0,1);

  x[1] ~ normal(0,10); // fat prior on x
  for (n in 2:N)
    x[n] ~ normal(f_off + f_trans * x[n-1], 1);
  y ~ normal(h_off + h_trans * x, h_noise);
}

No more constraints on parameters, but the scale of x[2:N] is
fixed to 1;  x[1] has a looser prior to deal with initial
conditions.

Here's an example of the simulated values originally supplied
by Dan Stowell (other than f_noise, which is now 1.0):

f_off <- 0.1;
f_trans <- -1.01;
f_noise <- 1.0;  # was 0.3;  (unit to identify)
h_off <- 1.2;
h_trans <- 0.4;
h_noise <- 0.7;
N <- 100;

Here's what's recovered by Stan (with f_noise set to 1); you can
see the reflection invariance:

f_off    -0.1     0.0 0.9   -1.8  -0.7  -0.1   0.6   1.8   369    1
f_trans  -1.0     0.0 0.0   -1.0  -1.0  -1.0  -1.0  -0.9   735    1
h_off     1.1     0.0 0.2    0.7   1.0   1.1   1.3   1.6   377    1
h_trans  -0.4     0.0 0.1   -0.6  -0.5  -0.4  -0.4  -0.3   145    1
h_noise   0.8     0.0 0.1    0.7   0.8   0.8   0.9   1.0   549    1
lp__    -83.7     0.6 9.6 -103.3 -90.0 -83.6 -77.0 -66.3   240    1

This was with 2500 post-warmup iterations, so effective sample size
still isn't great, but that seems to be the case with most time-series-like
models.

Fitting is still a bit unstable.  Without init=0, convergence is
not good.

With 100 data points and fairly tight priors, there's still large
posterior uncertainty.

Going to 1000 data points is problematic.  I think this may be partly
due to the simulated x values rising to 1e5 with the exponential
growth due to ftrans=-1.01.  With ftrans=0.8, it all fits very
tightly with N=1000.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Drawing from a posterior distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tim,

I am guessing you are thinking in terms of a Gibbs sampler, which while Bayesian is not Stanian. Stan evaluates the joint posterior and decides to accept proposals with a Metropolis-Hastings acceptance step where the proposal is generated in a somewhat complicated fashion using Hamiltonians. So, it doesn't make sense to draw a random proposal for a parameter inside the model block of a .stan file. I think the proposals in Stan are actually deterministic once you condition on the realization of the momentum, although there is randomness in whether the proposal is accepted.

In any event, it sounds like what you are trying to do would be to put a log-normal prior on the species-specific parameters where the location and scale of this log-normal distribution are fixed or perhaps are unknown parameters with informative priors. If so, you can just do that in the model block.

The generated quantities block is for auxiliary calculations that are not part of the model and in that case, drawing randomly from a posterior predictive distribution can be a reasonable thing to do.

Ben

messages.subject: something wrong with my cubic B-spline simulation/model
messages.subject_clean: something wrong with my cubic B-spline simulation/model
messages.body_plain:
>> On 6/13/13 12:31 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
 >>> Do we have B-splines?

On 6/16/13 4:08 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> It should be possible to implement splines with fixed numbers of knots right now.  We could implement some specialized
> functions which would make it more convenient and potentially faster but the basic functionality would remain the same.

We've been discussing cubic b-splines on the dev list,
but I thought I'd post my (failed?) attempt at fitting
the models here, because as Marcus noted, it shouldn't
require anything special.

Any help would be appreciated because I've already wasted
considerable time trying to get it to work (or maybe I
did and don't realize it --- see below).

I'm attaching

   * David Dunson's DRAFT section on cubic b-splines for the next
     edition of Bayesian data analysis (aka "BDA3").

   * my attempt to simulate data in R

   * my attempt to write a Stan model to fit it

I tried to keep the notation in R and Stan as close to that
of BDA3 as possible.

The two problems I'm having are:

   * the simulations don't look anything like Dunson's:

        - my simulations look like simple cubic functions,
          whereas Dunson's have many local minima and maxima

        - my simulations take all sorts of values outside of [0,1]
          for inputs in [0,1], whereas Dunson drew many simulations
          all of which took  values in [0,1] for inputs in [0,1]

        - I believe by "standard normal" he means Normal(0,1)
          for the coefficients

   * Stan isn't recovering the coefficients, despite reporting
     good R-hat and n_eff

        - or maybe this is the best we can do?  with only 2 knots
          and 10000 data points, it's getting the noise scale right
          and the params are within very very fat 95% intervals

Here are some comments on the BDA draft and how I got through
them (there may be errors in my reasoning here, of course).

The first problem I had is that the meaning of H
changes from the number of regression coefficients in
(20.1) to the number of knots later in the same paragraph.
So I couldn't tell what was going on in later figures when
they said H = 21.

I didn't understand the notation for the "positive part" of
a function, or even that that's what it was supposed to be:

   z_+ = 1_{z > 0}z

So I went searching.  I found the explanations in section 5.2 of Hastie
et al.'s  book much crisper mathematically in that I could follow its
definitions:

   http://www-stat.stanford.edu/~tibs/ElemStatLearn/

In particular, it cleared up the + notation as:

   f(x)_+ = max(0,f(x))

Thus I inferred that 1_{z > 0} was an indicator function in notation
I'd never seen before.  The post-multiplication by z is unfortunate
typographically.

BDA then continues with "...closely related alternative choice of
splines, which we find preferable, is the family of cubic B-splines'",
but it never precisely defines cubic B-splines.  It does provide an illustration
in figure 1 that I can't make heads or tails of (I think it's a bunch of overplotted
functions, but unlike the rest of BDA, the caption doesn't give any details).
The figure  says it was generated "with the bs() function R", but again
no details as to how.  Turns out bs() is a function in Hastie et al.'s
"splines" package, which is on CRAN, but which doesn't run in R 3.0.0.
(I'd add a citation to the BDA section).

Am I just simulating from the wrong model?  Is what I have not
cubic B-splines?  It looks like they are from Hastie et al., but then
Hastie et al. go on to define "natural cubic splines" in section 5.2.1.

Anyway, I think I'll leave this for someone else to do, as I need
to get back to actually coding Stan itself.

The next thing I would've done would've been to expand out the basis
explicitly and try to fit that directly using linear regression (that is,
not try to compute the splines in Stan).  But even if that worked, it
wouldn't solve the problem that my simulations look nothing at all like
Dunson's.

- Bob

Hi (again) Stan team,

Thanks again for the reply!

I am still trying to figure out what is going on with a positive definiteness problem for a covariance matrix. I get a non-fatal error every once in a while, and would like to track down exactly why I get this. Bob mentioned that we need strict positive definiteness. The error I am referring to is:

=====
Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal (really) issue (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Error in function stan::prob::multi_normal_log(d): Covariance matrix is not positive definite. ====

I added some print statements to my model block to figure out which parameter combinations are throwing this error. My (0,0) entry of the matrix matches the number printed in the error, so I'm pretty sure I've got the right parameter set... (Granted the printed output has a different number of significant digits than Stan uses, so my computations will differ slightly from those Stan does.)

I attached some code, data, and a text file of the printed output I get. I ran this using Rstan with my seed set to 11.

Model is a Gaussian Process model linked to multinomial count data. Covariance matrix is negative exponential, with three parameters that are used to construct it (eta, rho, sigma_sq).

Any thoughts as to what is going on? I'm wondering if I am just missing something obvious here ...

In case this helps:
> sessionInfo()
R version 2.15.2 (2012-10-26)

1.  There's a chapter that includes a section on measurement
error in the model and there's an entire chapter of Andrew's
Baysesian Data Analysis book on measurement error with many
more examples.

2.  As always, I'd recommend that you start with a simpler model
and work up to what you're trying to do.  For instance, define
the model without measurement error, then add a measurement
error component.  The purpose is to isolate where the problems
are one step at a time, because it's hard to debug a complex
model.

3.  There are (at least) two problems with the model you specified,
the relevant bits of which are:

data{
   ...

   vector          [n_spp] obsSGR_m  ; // mean SGR estimated for each species. already log-transformed (in R)
   vector<lower=0> [n_spp] obsSGR_sd ; // SD of SGR estimated for each species. bounded at 0 bc it's a SD

   ...

}
model {
    vector [n_spp] predSGR;         // predicted from trait values

    ....
    obsSGR_w_error <- lognormal_rng(obsSGR_m, obsSGR_sd);
    ...
    obsSGR_w_error ~ normal(predSGR, sigma_SGR);
    ...
}

Problem number one is that the _rng functions aren't available
in the model block --- only in generated quantities.   So you
need to define the "true" measurement as a parameter with appropriate
constraints.

I'm also confused about the intent of your model.  It looks
like you're using lognormal measurement error  In a typical
measurement error model, you'd have something like this:

   data {
      ... meas_with_error;
      ... meas_noise;
      ...
   }
   parameters {
      ... true_meas;
      ...
   }
   model {

     meas_with_error ~ foo(true_meas, meas_noise);

     true_meas ~ bar(...);

   }

This draws the observation meas_with_error from an
unknonw true_meas, and then uses the true_meas as if it
were data.

You put the errorful measurement on the left side twice, which
muddies the water a bit conceptually.  In Stan, putting the
same value on the left side of a sampling statement twice is
the same thing as giving it the product of the densities.

On the other hand, if foo() is the normal distribution, it can
be equivalent because

     a ~ normal(b,c)

has the same log probability as:

    b ~ normal(a,c).

And all Stan cares about is getting the log probability right.

- Bob

messages.subject: Conditional Logistic Regression in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

A few questions related to a conditional logistic regression.

1) Is there a way in Stan to model a conditional logistic regression?  (I didn't see it in the manual)

2) With a CLR, the posterior is a probability estimate of the outcome for each member of a group, with the within-group probabilities summing to 1.  With many draws from the posterior, I will effectively have many draws of possible probabilities. (I have N draws of probabilities for K members of a race.)   How would I then simulate outcomes?  What is the probability of member i winning?

3) I have probabilities of winning for each race member (from another model.)  It would be interesting to treat those as priors for a model in Stan.  However, I'm used to thinking about priors on the coefficients as drawn from some distribution, not actual point estimates of the outcomes.  How would I set that up in Stan?

Thanks in advance!

On Saturday, June 22, 2013 2:59:21 PM UTC-4, Noah wrote:
> A few questions related to a conditional logistic regression.
>
> 1) Is there a way in Stan to model a conditional logistic regression?  (I didn't see it in the manual)

I think Stan can do pretty much any regression, but the conditional logistic log-likelihood isn't programmed into Stan yet, so the log-likelihood would have to be evaluated using Stan code and manipulation of the lp__ symbol.

> 2) With a CLR, the posterior is a probability estimate of the outcome for each member of a group, with the within-group probabilities summing to 1.  With many draws from the posterior, I will effectively have many draws of possible probabilities. (I have N draws of probabilities for K members of a race.)  How would I then simulate outcomes?  What is the probability of member i winning?

There is a good explanation of the probabilities and the likelihood here

http://www.stata.com/support/faqs/statistics/within-group-collinearity-and-clogit/

To implement this in Stan, you will need to take logs to get the categorical log-likelihood and you probably want to use some of the log_sum_exp() tricks to prevent numerical overflow. In any event, once you get the posterior probabilities, you can just draw from categorical_rng() for each group.

> 3) I have probabilities of winning for each race member (from another model.)  It would be interesting to treat those as priors for a model in Stan.  However, I'm used to thinking about priors on the coefficients as drawn from some distribution, not actual point estimates of the outcomes.  How would I set that up in Stan?

Does your model have predictors? If so, it is going to be pretty tedious to analytically derive the distribution of the coefficients conditional on the probability of winning. In Stan, you proceed numerically by adjusting lp__ by the log absolute Jacobian determinant of the transformation from probabilities to coefficients, but this is difficult at best.

Ben

messages.subject: Translating a JAGS module for Stan?
messages.subject_clean: Translating a JAGS module for Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

For decades it has been known that human response data from experiments involving simple perceptual discriminations are very well fit by a "diffusion model" consisting of a Wiener process unfolding through time between two bounds (reaching a bound causes the process to terminate, determining a response and the response time). I'd like to use Stan to perform inference on a hierarchical version of such a model (aggregating data from multiple human subjects, each measured hundreds of times). Apparently there already exists code in the form of a JAGS module (http://sourceforge.net/projects/jags-wiener/) that implements the sort of model I'd like to implement. Any advice on how I should go about translating this for use with Stan? Or are there tools already in Stan that could be used to implement this sort of model?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

1.  If it's easier to define the joint density p(y,t), then
you could always just model both y and t and then forget
about y.  Basically, MCMC would do the integration for you.

2.  To implement Tuerlinckx's approach, we'd have to port the MATLAB
or Fortran iterative code to templated C++.  The derivatives would
be slow if many iterations are required.  If there were
a way to compute the derivatives directly (even if iterative),
that would be much faster.

3.  Next year, we'll be working on building in diff eq solvers
for implicit equations, but I'm not sure that'll help here.

- Bob

I've also been puzzled by trying to implement this model in Stan. If it helps the discussion along, I have some R code to simulate and illustrate this kind of model:

https://gist.github.com/crowding/5846850

That Tuerlinckx paper is pretty heady. Here's a simpler introduction to the topic: http://www.shadlenlab.columbia.edu/~mike/papers/mine/okinawa_chapter2006.pdf

For most of the questions the mathematical psychologists have about such models (e.g. are bounds time-varying, is a single decision variable enough, how to deal with N>2 choices), finding closed form solutions for the likelihood function is a fool's errand. In practice, what people do is discretize the response time and the decision variable(s) over a grid, for each distinct type of trial, and then numerically sum out the Fokker-Planck equation from there to get likelihoods.

That's also the best idea I have for implementing this model in Stan, but I'm not sure if the gradient calculations can cope with it.

(Other possibilities are making the noise an explicit vector parameter for each trial, which would lead to an explosion of parameters.)

Peter Meilstrup
Physiology and Biophysics
University of Washington

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Has anyone tried to install Rstan with 'clang++ -std=c++11 -stdlib=libc++' in R-devel on a Mac?

Thanks,
Rob J. Goedman
goe...@icloud.com

--------- DETAILS -------------

Following the standard route (CRAN builds, etc.) I have no problem with using Stan or Rstan.

Compiling stan with clang++ also works fine and finishes 'make o=0 test-unit' without any problems.

But recently I have been looking into compiling R and Rcpp, RcppArmadillo and RcppEigen using clang++ with the 2011 extensions. Rcpp, RcppArmadillo and RcppEigen all work and indeed I can compile lambda functions, say using Rstudio or using command line R on my Mac.

The next step was to try and compile Stan and Rstan using the same compiler flags.

The command line version of stan does generate, in addition to the 'warnings' I'd seen with just clang++, 'notes'  (e.g. lib/boost_1.53.0/boost/concept_check.hpp:521:15: note: in instantiation of member function),  but seems to work in the end (see stan-output.txt below, all the way at the end and sample.csv), although 'make o=0 test-unit' now fails (see test-output.txt).

Installation of Rstan produces similar error messages as making stan for command line usage, but now will fail as illustrated in bernoulli.txt.

I couldn't figure out how to present an easier, reproducible example.

What vector[1] is telling you is that tau is declared as an
array of vectors.  The cauchy wants either vectors, row
vectors, or 1D arrays.

The following will do what you intended:

   for (i in 1:p)
     tau[i] ~ cauchy(0,sigma_tau);

Given that tau[i] is an ordered vector, I'm not exactly
sure what that implies for the distribution of tau because
of the order constraints.

You could provide a proper model with a prior on tau[1]
and (tau[p] - tau[1]), with the interior points uniform,
or you can put a prior on tau[1] and then all the differences.
Either way, you'd need to account for the log Jacobian implicated
by the variable transform.

I was asking Andrew about what we should be using for priors
here, but don't recall his response.

- Bob

Sorry, that's not going to work, because the unit_vector
isn't standardized to have mean(x_raw) = 0, so that means
there's no guarantee that var(x_raw) = 1 / K, just because
sum(x_raw^2) = 1.  It would require:

Back to the drawing board.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
This behaviour typically suggests that your posterior has multiple modes.  A stronger prior could help alleviate this.  Alternatively, longer simulations may be useful if the stronger priors are inappropriate or undesirable.

One thing that is suspicious to me is that the jump seems to happen immediately after the warmup period ends.  What version of Stan are you using?  Have you looked at the stepsizes that it's using?

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure how your code got this far.

Stan isn't BUGS and uses a different syntax for
arrays and vectors and matrices.  There are many examples
in the manual along with full definitions.

Are you sure the code attached led to this error?  The
Stan parser should gripe about this illegal declaration:

   real prob[n, p, 1:4];

Unlike R and BUGS, Stan doesn't have array slicing with
the ":" operator.

The line you cite is also illegal for the same reason:

   y[i,j]~categorical(prob[i,j,1:K[j]])

You either need to use a loop or use the entire slice.

Stan has local variables, and also can have expressions
inside distributions, so it's otherwise not as restrictive
as BUGS (more like JAGS).

In general, you can debug these models with these error
messages by looking at where the error message is pointing
and checking your syntax against the definition of what's
allowed in the manual.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Strange errors with very simple model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Strange errors with very simple model
messages.body_plain:
The problem isn't in the dot product syntax, but that
you are trying to assign a value to a parameter, which
Stan doesn't allow.

Variables can only be assigned in the block in which
they are declared, and there are no statements allowed
in a parameters block, so parameters can't be assigned to
anywhere.  You can define eta as a transformed parameter
and assign to it in the transformed parameters block.

If you need something that can be assigned to, use a local
variable. For example, this is well formed, as would be
replacing "model" with "transformed parameters":

   parameters {
     matrix[3,2] A;
     vector[2] B;
     ...
   }
   model {
     real C;
     C <- dot_product(A[1],B);
     ...
   }

The only difference between transformed parameters and local variables
in the model block is that transformed parameters are returned along
with parameters as output by the sampler (or optimizer).

You can also declare A as an array of (row) vectors, which
is a bit more efficient as it doesn't require allocation and
copies (matrices are stored column-major, so you can't easily
slice out a row w/o a non-memory-local copy).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Crashing STAN violating assert() in eigen
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Crashing STAN violating assert() in eigen
messages.body_plain:
Can the compiler really re-order in such a way that an
assert() doesn't stop the program where it occurs?  I know
unspecified-by-the-standard behavior can change, but I'd
think order of statements would be guaranteed.

assert() is, of course, not an exception.  If we get an
exception, it'll percolate up right away.  Nothing catches
it other than the sampler.  Again, I'd expect the error to happen
right away and that behavior to be guaranteed.

Also, behavior here should depend on debug status in R.
In Stan 1.3.0, I believe it's still possible to get an assert
if you're using set_cppo("fast") [which is the default].

This should change in Stan 2.0, so that the only way you
can crash R is if you configure a third mode that turns off
our error checking and lets thing go through to Eigen's library.

We don't want anything crashing RStan in debug() mode.  In fact,
for 2.0, I really don't want anything crashing RStan in any mode
unless we explicitly warn the user when they configure.

- Bob
