> Well, the limited timing test is not very encouraging: 100 iterations actually ran in roughly 60 seconds with
> for (n in 1:n_cases) {
>     for (k in 1:n_hidden) {
>       hidden_nl[k,n] <- tanh(hidden[k,n]);
>     }
>   }

There are at least three senses of "vectorizing" in Stan.

Does the function, tanh() in this case, accept a vector as an argument an apply the function elementwise? Apparently not, but that doesn't really affect the speed. If there were a tanh() function that took a vector or matrix as an argument, then it would just do what you did above by looping over the rows and columns and calling the corresponding scalar function. It would be nice if the user didn't need to type as much, but either way it gets compiled to a C++ loop.
In addition to 1), does the function do something clever with the derivatives? For a lot of the probability distributions, the answer is yes, but not so much for tanh()
Does the function utilize hardware vectorization? This is a major concept for Eigen but doesn't get used much in Stan because the hardware can't vectorize the custom scalar types that Stan uses and Stan currently doesn't do that much with plain doubles.
So, I wouldn't really expect anything to speed tanh() up except by writing a more efficient implementation of tanh(). The existing one

https://raw.github.com/stan-dev/stan/develop/src/stan/agrad/rev/tanh.hpp

is not great because it calculates std::tanh() and then std::cosh() to get the derivative. It might be faster (and should be more stable) if we calculated

log(1 - exp(-2x)) == log_diff_exp(0, -2 * x) = a
log(1 + exp(-2x)) == log_sum_exp( 0, -2 * x) = b
tanh(x) == exp( a - b )
cosh(x) == exp( b - LOG2 + x )

Ben

Backprop is exactly (reverse mode) autodiff, so there wouldn't be any benefit there.  I'm guessing you're running into the same problem that Neal ran into with BNN in his thesis.  Because the net is highly correlated a small change in parameters will yield a huge change in density, but because on average HMC transitions can only vary the log density by (dimension) / 2 the parameter movement will be small and you'll basically have a random walk.  Riemannian HMC fixes this automatically, but the quickest solution is to employ the "Matt trick" to remove the correlations in the first place.

On 6/24/13 1:40 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> What is the use case here? Standardization could be useful for data, but I have a harder time thinking of when it would
> be useful for a parameter. And if it were used for a parameter, I have a harder time thinking of a case where we would
> need to do more than use a prior whose mean is zero.

I'll cite chapter and verse, though it's not clear it'll be very
useful :-)

Gelman and Hill, Chapter 14, Section 14.3, subsection "An ideal-point model for Supreme
Court voting", says, with respect to identification,

   We can resolve both these indeterminancies by constraining
   the alpha[j]'s to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1

and then finishes the sentence with,

   or, in a multilevel context, by giving the alpha[j] a N(0,1) distribution.

For the simple IRT models in the previous subsection, they
suggest centering w/o scale standardization.

Of course, if we only need to use the transformed parameter on the right side
of later statements, then we can just use

    y <- (y_raw - mean(y_raw)) / sd(y_raw)

But again, I'm not sure what the implications are for the prior -- it's a pretty
involved set of derivatives in the Jacobian.

- Bob

       of "the alpha", "the alpha[j]", or "the alpha[j]s" (no possessive)
       throughout.

messages.body_plain:
On 6/25/13 11:11 AM, Julien Cornebise wrote:
> ...

> I have a somewhat stupid follow-up: is there a way to give Stan closed-form the derivatives to use (i.e. use NUTS with
> manual derivatives), since they are easy-ish in neural net models with the so-called "backpropagation", and would that
> be likely to speed anything up, or is AFD always using the most efficient way of computing the derivatives?

To elaborate a bit on Michael's answer, it depends what the model is.
Our auto-diff is pretty efficient, but there are certainly cases
where it can be made more efficient and more arithmetically stable.

For example, rather than doing poisson(exp(alpha)), we have a
distribution poisson_log(alpha) =def= poisson(exp(alpha)), and we
have customized the derivatives for poisson_log.

The auto-diff needs to be defined in C++ along the same lines
as our other functions.

In the particular case of logistic regression, even if we had
a custom auto-diffed GLM distribution

    y ~ logistic_regression(x, beta);

where y is an N-vector, x is an (N x K) predictor matrix,
and beta is a K-vector, even a careful implementation probably
wouldn't be much more efficient than the current idiom:

    y ~ bernoulli_logit(x * beta);

The main saving comes from eliminating intermediate expressions by
reducing (partially evaluating in computational terms) analytically.

- Bob

> Court voting", says, with respect to identification,
>
>    We can resolve both these indeterminancies by constraining
>    the alpha[j]'s to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1

>
> and then finishes the sentence with,
>
>    or, in a multilevel context, by giving the alpha[j] a N(0,1) distribution.

My understanding is that, in a unidimensional model, the posterior distribution will be curved everywhere as long as the prior distribution on the ideal points has a fixed mean and standard deviation. In other words, in that case, we don't need a variable type that has mean zero and unit standard deviation, we just need a iid normal(0,1) prior on a plain vector[N]. There is still an indeterminacy with the sign in the sense that you can multiply the ideal points by -1 and the coefficients by -1 and get the same predictions for the outcomes, but that can be overcome by constraining some ideal point to be positive.

The multidimensional case is harder. Again, you can curve the posterior with a multi_normal(zeros, Sigma) prior where Sigma is a correlation matrix, and again you have the small problem that you can multiply by -1. The bigger problem is that you can do a symmetric permutation of the rows and columns of Sigma and the same permutation of the columns of the ideal points and get the same predictions for the outcomes. In this case, you really want some sort of an ordering constraint on some of the coefficients.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, June 25, 2013 4:52:20 AM UTC-4, Dieter Menne wrote:
> Whenever I do summary(..) in R, I expect some output to be printed by default when no assignment takes place. rstan is the only package I know of that behaves different, i.e. an explicit print(summary(mr.stan))  or (summary(mr.stan)) is needed.
>
> When nothing comes out of summary(mr.stan), I intuitively do a sink() to counteract any suspected black hole. The same is true for other functions, such as extract, but it is most unexpected for summary.
>
> Is there a reason for this? Did I miss something in the documentation? I personally believe that streamlining this to standard R behavior would be nice.

A lot of methods defined by rstan return things invisibly, meaning that the object is created if you assign to it and not otherwise. So,

s <- summary(fit)

creates an object called s whereas

summary(fit)

does all the same calculations but does not create an object.

Using invisible() so heavily is atypical for an R package, but Andrew never feels bound by R conventions. I think in this case, it is intended to discourage users from calling things like summary() unless they need the components of the list that summary produces. The canonical way to examine the output is to use the print() or show() methods on the fit object or just type

fit

which implicitly calls show() and then print(). Again, this is contrary to the rest of R where calling print() or show() would typically tell you some basic information about the model and summary() would give you coefficients, standard errors, etc. So, I would agree with you that this behavior is not great, but it is intentional.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, June 25, 2013 4:58:55 PM UTC-4, Rob J Goedman wrote:
> I've attached 8schools.R below, but haven't changed that file for a while now and it runs fine with Rstan using CRAN R-3.0.1.
>
> I'll try what happens with other levels of optimization when compiling stan.
>
> What surprises me is:
>
> 1)        Compiling stan and installing Rstan both create error messages as below (related to templating in the boost package?).
>
> 2)        But while stan works, e.g. the standard bivariate example in src/models/... works fine, Rstan can't compile a 'similar' input file (bivariate.R, added below) with the console displaying:

If the parser (stanc) is compiled with optimization and you use C++11, then there will be a parser failure along the lines of what you found. There is some debate about whether this behavior is a bug on boost's part. Command-line Stan has O_STANC distinct from O so that you can compile stanc without optimization and the rest of stan with optimization. But rstan uses one optimization level for everything.

Maybe rstan 2.0 will make this distinction. But for now, if you want to use C++-11, you are pretty much stuck with command-line Stan. However, Stan doesn't use any C++-11 features, so I doubt it would have a noticeable effect on performance. We've been trying to get compliant with the C++11 standard for a while but mostly to make sure that we don't have any undefined behavior.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: question about mixture distributions
messages.body_plain:
On 6/25/13 9:33 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Tuesday, June 25, 2013 9:27:40 PM UTC-4, xin cheng wrote:
>
>     I am a new-comer to Stan. Current I am working on a project, and I am wondering if I could use Stan to solve my problem:
>
>     the model is like this:
>
>     y|x ~ x*beta + normal(0,1);
>     m ~ double-expoential (0.5);
>     beta <- m* I(abs(m)>=1) ;  //  the distribution of beta is a mixture of point mass at 0, and double exponential dist
>     when abs(beta) >=1;
>
> There is no inclusion function, but you can accomplish the same thing with if_else, like
>
> |
> beta <- if_else(abs(m) >= 1, m, 0.0);
> |

I take it in the comment you meant "abs(m) >= 1" to match the code.

Setting aside Andrew's objection to the modeling decision,
the way Ben suggests is the right way to do this for efficiency,
and also, I believe, for clarity.

You could also translate directly as:

    beta <- m * (abs(m) >= 1);

The conditional expression (abs(m) >= 1) evaluates to integer
1 if the condition is true and 0 otherwise.  As long as m is real,
the integer gets promoted to a real.

It's also going to be a bit tricky to model.  You'll need
to write the sampling statement in Stan as:

     y ~ normal(if_else(abs(m) >= 1, m, 0.0), 1);
     m ~ double_exponential(0, 0.5);

The suboptimality Ben was alluding to is because of the lack of
derivative for abs(m) < 1;  there's also the problem of the
discontinuity at 1, so it's not clear you'll be able to smoothly
transition.

- Bob

It works if stanc is not compiled with optimization, which is the default for command-line Stan. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Vectorized if_else?
messages.body_plain:
On 6/26/13 10:18 AM, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> I'm working on vectorizing my implementation of a hierarchical linear ballistic accumulator model of human response time
> and accuracy.
>
> My latest .stan file is here: https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/5867645
>
> I'm getting errors (line 103) seemingly because my assumption that if_else() can be used in the same vectorized manner
> as ifelse() in R is faulty.

The appendix of the manual lists all of the available
function signatures.  if_else() is not vectorized yet.

We'll eventually get around to vectorizing everything.

Here's the error:
>
>      no matches for function name="if_else"
>          arg 0 type=vector
>          arg 1 type=vector
>          arg 2 type=vector
>      available function signatures for if_else:
>      0.  if_else(int, real, real) : real
>
>
> Is there any workaround?

Just declare a variable to hold the result and assign in a loop.

Assuming t and f are vectors and c a vector you want to test
for zero, then

    ...if_else(c,t,f)...

   {
      vector[size(c)] y;
      for (i in 1:size(c))
        y[x] = if_else(c[i] == 0, t[i], f[i]);

      ...y...
   }

This declares y as a local variable in whatever loop you need it.

It'd be more efficient rather than to define t and f to just
build up y in a loop using the conditional if { ... } else { ... }.
You don't want to create variables you don't use, as it's extra
overhead for auto-diff.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] "real a[2]" vs "vector[2] a" ?
messages.body_plain:
They have slightly different ops defined on them, but
we'll be unifying those in the future.

In general, you should prefer vector unless there's an
operation that only works on arrays.  The reason is that
the vector/matrix/linear-algebra ops are only defined on
vectors and all the multivariate distributions are defined
in terms of vector/matrix parameters.

Also note that arrays of row vectors behave very similarly
to matrices:

    matrix[M,N] x;

vs.

    row_vector[N] x[M];

The latter array-based version has faster row access if you
use x[m] (which is row m of the matrix x).

- Bob

On Wed, Jun 26, 2013 at 12:25 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:

> If I have the code:
>
>     vector[2] a;
>     vector[2] b;
>     a[1] <- 1;
>     a[2] <- 2;
>     b <- normal_log(a,0,1);
>
> I get the parser error:
>
>     base type mismatch in assignment; left variable=dummy; left base type=vector; right base type=real
>
> If I change to:
>
>     vector[2] a;
>     real b[2];
>     a[1] <- 1;
>     a[2] <- 2;
>     b <- normal_log(a,0,1)
>
> I get another parser error:
>
>     mismatched dimensions on left- and right-hand side of assignment; left dims=1; right dims=0
>
> I'm aware that I can loop over the indices of a to assign each element of b, but I'm of the (possibly mistaken?) impression from my R experiences that such loops are inefficient relative to vectorized approaches. This, however, presumes that a vectorized approach exists... does it?

The issue is that the return of normal_log(a, 0, 1) is going to be real. A single value. In this case, the return of:
normal_log(a,0,1)

is equivalent to:
normal_log(a[1],0,1) + normal_log(a[2],0,1)

Hopefully that clears up the confusion.

What are you trying to do? If you want to store the unnormalized log of the normal pdf evaluated for each element of a, you could loop, but I'm not sure if that's what you actually want to do. From the modeling language, I don't think there is a way to ask for the normalized log pdf value for any of our distributions, so for this case, it will return -a[1]^2/2 - a[2]^2/2.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] trouble storing results from normal_log() when vectorized
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] trouble storing results from normal_log() when vectorized
messages.body_plain:
On 6/26/13 12:25 PM, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> If I have the code:
>
>      vector[2] a;
>      vector[2] b;
>      a[1] <- 1;
>      a[2] <- 2;
>      b <- normal_log(a,0,1);
>
> I get the parser error:
>
>      base type mismatch in assignment; left variable=dummy; left base type=vector; right base type=real

The problem is that normal_log() returns a real, but b is a vector.
It adds all the log probabilities.

> If I change to:
>
>      vector[2] a;
>      real b[2];
>      a[1] <- 1;
>      a[2] <- 2;
>      b <- normal_log(a,0,1)
>
> I get another parser error:
>
>      mismatched dimensions on left- and right-hand side of assignment; left dims=1; right dims=0

Same problem, only for arrays.

> I'm aware that I can loop over the indices of a to assign each element of b, but I'm of the (possibly mistaken?)
> impression from my R experiences that such loops are inefficient relative to vectorized approaches. This, however,
> presumes that a vectorized approach exists... does it?

Unlike R, Stan is compiled.  So basic loops, assignments, etc., are very
cheap.  In fact, they're usually more efficient than the way R vectorizes
everything because you don't need to allocate temporary variables to
hold intermediate variables.

Having said that, you do want to vectorize calls to functions involving
parameters because the auto-diff is in some sense interpreted in Stan.
But given that normal_log returns a single log probability, there's no
alternative but to do a loop here.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Jun 25, 2013, at 7:25 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Tuesday, June 25, 2013 10:21:11 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Yikes.  I didn't realize it didn't work as opposed to just
> > issuing a warning.
>
> It works if stanc is not compiled with optimization, which is the default for command-line Stan. RStan has never done different optimization levels for stanc and the rest, because it either used what was in ~/.R/Makevars or did -O3. With the most recent version of R, we can actually behave like Stan does.
>
> But I can't think of a reason why an RStan user should care about using --std=c++11 anyway.

Agreed. For another project I want to use Rcpp/RcppArmadillo with C++11 extensions and ran into the issue.

Your and Bob's answers confirmed the behavior I noticed. Compiling Rstan with -O0 indeed solves the issue!

Thanks again for your help, regards,
Rob J. Goedman
goe...@icloud.com

faster.

could just diagnose whether the problem was ours or in the
Boost Spirit Qi parser lib.

- Bob

messages.subject: Stan 2.0 e.t.a.
messages.body_plain:
On 6/26/13 2:01 PM, Brendan wrote:
...

> Just out of interest, do you guys have any rough ideas about when 2.0 might be ready?

Maybe in a couple of weeks, but no promises.

We're making a lot of changes, so we want to make sure
everything works smoothly so we don't have to make even more
changes going forward.

The development branch on GitHub is stable under our new
development process, but I'll warn you that the command structure
will change.  After that change, RStan will follow, and we'll
be pretty much ready to release.  Much of the doc is going to
need to change, too.

Overall, the interface through RStan shouldn't be that
different.  It'll mainly be an under-the-hood change with
more options in terms of samplers, adaptation, and optimization.

We might roll out a beta first to work out the kinks with
a wider pool of users.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help with optimization?
messages.body_plain:
Here are a couple tips to speed things up:

- Compute 1-accuracy[i] and reuse it instead of recomputing it 3 times
- As above, for many of the computations in that loop they are the same for each subject.  Precompute them for each subject in an array and then reference them in the loop.
- If L is large, instead of incrementing lp__ each time, create a vector[2*L] lpterms and set it's entry in the loop.  Then at the end of the loop write: lp__ <- lp__ + sum(lpterms);

The last one is probably your best bet for a quick win.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: timing scaling
messages.body_plain:
Hi stan team,

I've been playing with a spatial predictive process model, and find that when my number of iterations get high (above about 70) the time it takes to execute the program increases significantly. To try to do some profiling I compiled with the -pg flag, and can see that the number of calls to functions in the stan::agrad namespace increase in a huge way when I go from 70 to 100 iterations (including log_prob_poly, mdivide_left_vv_vari, etc.). I assume this significant increase in function calls is in part what seems to really bog down my runs if my number of iterations gets over 70.

The data set is fairly large -  2261 spatial cells, but with only 19 knots (so sampling happens with a covariance matrix that is 19 x 19). It is attached in a compressed bzipped format. I haven't noticed this behavior with small data sets that I tried the code with (hence the large attached data set), but perhaps it is just more exaggerated here.

This is what I find when I run the executable with a seed=1234 for the same data set.

70 iterations
==========
Elapsed time: 60.96 seconds
Number of calls to log_prob_poly: 951

100 iterations
==========
Elapsed time: 1185 seconds (19.75 minutes)
Number of calls to log_prob_poly: 23984

Attached the stan file, data file, and the first 20 lines of the output from the profiler for both the 70 and 100 iteration runs are attached.

Any ideas why this happens if my number of iterations get above about 70? It's not really intuitive to me why this would happen, but I am not all that familiar with how the NUTS algorithm is implemented.

Thanks again for all your help!

Andria

Thanks for providing details.

Before looking at timing results for iterations, I would check to make sure the model is converging. I didn't follow through with all your seeds, but with seed=1234, Stan is not effectively sampling any of the parameters (eta, rho, sigma_sq, mu, alpha) at 70 iterations. Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] timing scaling
messages.body_plain:
What's most likely happening is that adaptation is figuring
out that it needs a smaller step size, which in turn leads to
more steps per iteration.   You can investigate this and the number
of steps (exp(treedepth)).   The exact iteration numbers at which this happens
may change in the future, but you should continue to see similar
effects.  This is the intended behavior.

As Daniel said, you really want to measure n_eff/second, which we
are going to include in the ouptut in v2.0.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 6/27/13 6:44 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, June 27, 2013 6:06:07 PM UTC-4, Andrew Lim wrote:

...

> Certainly large arrays in the parameters block would tend to be slow because then you have a lot of parameters that Stan
> needs to track the gradient of. A large array in transformed parameters or locally in the model block usually isn't a
> major time suck compared to the auto-differentiation.

Right.  But the transformed parameters do add auto-diff variables
to the stack (and hence cause constructors to be called and a virtual
function to be called during autodiff).  But in this case, these would
have to be calculated anyway for the linear predictors.

> However, if you do it in transformed parameters, then it has to
> write a lot of columns in the csv file. In most cases, the linear predictor isn't interesting enough to store and if it
> were needed, then it could easily be reconstructed in R afterward.
>
> You do want to utilize matrix algebra whenever possible because those operations tend to be those where someone (usually
> Marcus) has done some performance optimizations. But that holds no matter what block you do it in.

It's mainly an issue for auto-diff variables (parameters, transformed
parameters, or local variables in transformed parameters or model).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, June 28, 2013 3:17:52 PM UTC-4, Andria Dawson wrote:
> Hi Daniel and Ben,

That was Bob. This is Ben for the first time on this thread.

> So if I understand correctly, this just means that in the 100 iterations case the number of steps per iteration is greater which explains why it takes more time? If my tree depth is say 8 for an iteration, does that mean I expect to call log_prob_poly exp(8) times (or some factor of exp(8))? (Sorry if that's a silly questions, I really am a NUTS newbie.)

Yes, the number of times the log posterior is evaluated depends on the treedepth when constructing a new proposal for the parameters. This is one reason why you should calculate quantities that are interesting but not needed for the log posterior in the generated quantities block. The generated quantities block is only evaluated once per proposal, while the transformed parameters block and the model block are evaluated every time the log posterior is evaluated.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Initialization failed after 100 attempts (NaN rejection)
messages.body_plain:
2013/6/28 Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com>:

> On 6/28/13 5:30 AM, Dan Stowell wrote:
>>
>> Hi all,
>>
>> The following model gets consistently rejected on initialisation:
>> https://gist.github.com/danstowell/5883463
>
>
> Thanks for providign the code.  One problem is the way you
> start the model:
>
> --------------------------------------------
>       model {
>         vector[D] newgen_means[N];
>         vector[D] newgen_stdvs[N];
>         vector[D] gen_means[N];
>         vector[D] gen_stdvs[N];
>
>         changeness ~ beta(0.6, 0.8);
>
>         // each datum is associated with its own generating gaussian
>         // Common prior for the brandnew
>         for (n in 1:N){
>                 newgen_means[n] ~ normal(0.0, 100.0);
>                 newgen_stdvs[n] ~ exponential(2.0);
>         }
> -----------------------------------------
>
> This won't work in Stan because you are using newgen_means[n] before
> you define it.  You declare the local variable, but don't give it
> a value.
>
> If you want to sample these values, they need to be declared
> as parameters.  And newgen_stdvs needs to be declared with the
> constraint lower=0.
>
> The ~ doesn't mean randomly generate the left-hand side from the
> distribution on the right hand side.  For instance, your first line
> is equivalent to:
>
>    lp__ <- lp__ + normal_log(newgen_means[n], 0, 100);
>
> where normal_log() is the built-in normal log density function.

Bob, thanks for that. I had initially specified those as parameters,
then moved them down to be local variables, without spotting the big
difference that makes wrt sampling. The code works now. (gist updated,
in case anyone's interested.)

Best
Dan
--
http://www.mcld.co.uk

messages.subject: Randomness during adapting causing slow sampling for chains in parallel?
messages.subject_clean: Randomness during adapting causing slow sampling for chains in parallel?
messages.body_plain:
What sort of randomness is there during the adapt phase? Could this be a cause for slowness in sampling between chains?

I have two very different types of models that I've encountered slowness in some chains when sampling from 3 chains in parallel. Both models have somewhere between 50k-100k sample sizes, some form of a normal likelihood, so nothing too crazy in either case, yet in both cases I find that one chain finishes sampling much faster than the other two.

My sense is that this caused by some sort of randomness at the start of the adapt phase in each chain. Is there anyway to monitor this, or possibly set some sort of initial values in hopes of having all chains sample at the faster rate?

Thanks for any insight!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Randomness during adapting causing slow sampling for chains in parallel?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Randomness during adapting causing slow sampling for chains in parallel?
messages.body_plain:
On 6/30/13 6:18 PM, Ryan wrote:
> What sort of randomness is there during the adapt phase?

If you don't specify initial values, those are initialized
between -2 and 2 uniformly on the unconstrained scale (constrained
variables are transformed to unconstrained scales automatically).

Then NUTS is run during adaptation, and that has several kinds
of built-in randomness, including initial momentum and the directions
in which to update and a final Metropolis reject step.

> Could this be a cause for slowness in sampling between chains?

Yes.

> I have two very different types of models that I've encountered slowness in some chains when sampling from 3 chains in
> parallel. Both models have somewhere between 50k-100k sample sizes, some form of a normal likelihood, so nothing too
> crazy in either case, yet in both cases I find that one chain finishes sampling much faster than the other two.

We've noticed that, too, and have been considering
time-based evaluation with appropriate weighting
among the chains.

Do all of the chains get to the same place eventually
in terms of the quantiles (or mean and sd).

> My sense is that this caused by some sort of randomness at the start of the adapt phase in each chain. Is there anyway
> to monitor this, or possibly set some sort of initial values in hopes of having all chains sample at the faster rate?

Yes, you can provide initial values for each chain.  If
they all start in the same place, they're much more likely
to all run at roughly the same speed, but you lose the
benefit of the conservative convergence diagnostics.

- Bob
